unit.unitOverview: Being lost is uncomfortable in any language and worse in one you are still learning, because the moment you most need to ask is the moment you least want to. This unit gives you the words for movement, the shape of a route, and one polite sentence for stopping a stranger. It ends with a set of written directions, because the ones you are given on paper are often clearer than the ones you are given out loud, and knowing how to read them saves you from asking twice.
unit.learningPath:
Read and listen to the Lesson. There are three patterns.
Open Patterns. Card 2 is the one to practise until it is automatic.
Learn the words. Twenty-nine, in five groups.
Read the three texts aloud. The third is a how-to-find-us notice.
Do the Practice. Practice 5 asks you to write directions to where you live.
Record yourself asking the way and giving a route.
Take the quiz, then update My progress.

visual.lectureScript:
This unit is about getting somewhere, and it needs less new grammar than you might expect, because you already have most of it.
In Unit 2 you learned where things are — in, on, under, behind, next to, between. Those describe things that are not moving. This unit adds the words for things that ARE moving, and there are about six of them.
Along. You go along a street — following its length.
Past. You go past a bank — you pass it and keep going. This one is useful because directions are often given by what you pass rather than where you turn.
Across. You go across a road — from one side to the other.
Through. You go through a park or through a door — in one side and out of the other.
Towards. You go towards the station — in its direction, not necessarily all the way there.
And round. You go round the corner, round the roundabout.
Second pattern is the shape of a route, and this is the one to practise until it arrives without thinking.
A route in English is a small number of instructions in order, and they use the imperative — the form you already know from Units 3 and 6. You are not learning a new grammar here. You are learning which verbs go in it.
Go straight on. Turn left. Turn right. Take the first turning on the left. Take the second on the right. Cross the road. Follow the signs. Continue for about two hundred metres.
And then, at the end, the position: it is on your left. It is on the corner. It is opposite the bank. It is next to the post office.
Notice the shape. Movements first, in order, and the position last. That is how English gives a route, and if you follow that shape you will be understood even when individual words go wrong.
One very useful thing. Directions in English are often given by landmarks rather than distances. Not go for three hundred metres, but go past the school and it is after the second set of traffic lights. If you are asking, a landmark answer is easier to follow than a distance answer, and if you are giving, a landmark answer is kinder.
Third pattern: how to stop somebody and ask. One sentence, learned properly.
Excuse me, could you tell me the way to the station?
Or shorter: Excuse me, where is the station, please?
Excuse me is how you begin. It is not an apology — it is the word that opens the conversation, and without it a question to a stranger sounds abrupt.
Could you is more polite than can you. Both are fine. Could is softer and it costs you nothing.
And then the part most learners forget: after they answer, say it back. So, straight on and then left at the lights? People will confirm or correct you, and either way you now know. Asking twice is normal. Walking the wrong way for ten minutes is worse.
Go to Patterns.

readings.title: Ask Early, and Say It Back
readings.passageScript:
Two habits make being lost much shorter, and neither of them is about grammar.
The first is to ask early. Most people walk for ten minutes hoping it will become obvious, and then ask. Ask at two minutes instead. You are less far from where you started, the person you ask is more likely to know, and you have lost two minutes rather than twelve.
The second is to say it back. When somebody has given you directions, repeat them. So, straight on, past the bank, and then left at the lights? They will say yes, or they will correct one part of it, and either way you now have it.
This matters more than it sounds. Directions are usually given quickly and in one breath, and even people listening in their own language lose the third instruction. Repeating is not a sign that your English is weak. Watch two people who share a language do it — the second one repeats the directions back almost every time.
One more thing. If somebody gives you a long route with five turnings, ask for less. Just the first part — where do I go first? Most people give too much detail because they are trying to help. You can ask again later, from somewhere closer.

readings.title: Landmarks Beat Distances
readings.passageScript:
There are two ways to give directions and one of them is much easier to follow.
By distance: go for three hundred metres, then turn left, then continue for another hundred.
By landmark: go past the school, turn left at the traffic lights, and it is opposite the bank.
The second is better for almost everybody. Nobody can judge three hundred metres while walking. Everybody can see a school.
So when you give directions, use what a person will actually see. Turn at the lights, not turn after eighty metres. Go past the market, not continue for two minutes.
And when you ask, you can steer the answer. Is it near the station? Do I pass anything I would recognise? Those questions ask for landmarks and usually get them.
One warning about distances given in time. Ten minutes means ten minutes for the person speaking. Somebody who walks that route every day walks it faster than you will while looking for it. Add half again to any time you are given and you will be less surprised.
And if you are told it is straight ahead, you cannot miss it — you probably can. That sentence is almost always said about something that is easy to walk past. Ask what is next to it.

readings.passageScript:
HOW TO FIND US
Northfield Community Centre
42 Park Road

BY BUS
  Routes 6, 14 and 22 stop on Station Road.
  From the bus stop, walk along Station Road
  towards the traffic lights. Cross at the
  crossing and turn right into Park Road.
  We are 200 metres along, opposite the bank.
  About 5 minutes.

BY TRAIN
  Northfield station. Leave by the SOUTH exit
  (the north exit is closed for building work
  until September). Turn left, go past the car
  park, then take the second turning on the
  right. About 12 minutes.

BY CAR
  There is no parking at the centre.
  The nearest car park is on Mill Street,
  a 4-minute walk. Free after 18:00.

ENTRANCES
  Main entrance: Park Road. Open 09:00-17:00.
  After 17:00 use the side entrance in the
  car park, and press the bell.

  Step-free access is at the side entrance
  only.

If you are lost, telephone 0300 774 2318.

across   one side to the other         go across the road
through  in one side, out the other    go through the park
towards  in its direction              walk towards the station
round    following a curve             go round the corner

Still / moving:
  The bank is next to the post office.  (still — Unit 2)
  Go past the bank.                     (moving)
grammar.workedExample:
You must get to the other side of a road. Which word?
1. Are you following its length, or getting to the other side? The other side.
2. One side to the other is across.
3. Result: Go across the road.
Now the opposite case: you are walking down the road, not crossing it. Following its length is along — go along the road.
Across and along are the two people mix up, and the test is the same each time: are you crossing it or following it?
grammar.commonMistake: Using in and on for movement — go in the park when you mean go through the park. In and on describe a position, not a journey. If something is moving, one of the six words on this card is what you need.

grammar.title: Giving a route
grammar.explanation: A route has a fixed shape in English: the movements in order, and then the position at the end. The grammar is the imperative, which you already know from Units 3 and 6 — what is new is which verbs go in it and how they are ordered.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
MOVEMENTS, in order:
  Go straight on.
  Turn left / right.
  Take the first turning on the left.
  Cross the road.
  Go past the bank.
  Continue for about 200 metres.

POSITION, at the end:
  It is on your left.
  It is on the corner.
  It is opposite the bank.

Movements first. Position last. Always.
grammar.workedExample:
Give a route: out of the station, along the road, second right, and the place faces the bank.
1. List the movements in the order they happen.
2. Turn each into an imperative — the verb first, nobody named.
3. Put the position at the very end.
Go out of the station and turn left.
Go along the road for about five minutes.
Take the second turning on the right.
It is opposite the bank.
Four sentences, three of them movements and one of them a position. If you put the position in the middle, the listener stops walking and starts looking.
grammar.commonMistake: Giving too much at once. Five turnings in one breath cannot be held by anybody, in any language. Give three steps, then say ask again from there. That is more useful than a complete route the person forgets halfway through.
grammar.memoryTip: Movements in order, position last, three steps at a time.

Go along this street.
Go past the bank.
Cross at the traffic lights.
Take the first turning on the left.
It is opposite the post office.
The position must be last. The order of the middle steps could vary — crossing before or after the bank both work — but going along the street has to come first and the position has to come last.

grammar.title: Excuse me, could you tell me …?
grammar.explanation: One sentence for stopping a stranger, learned properly. The parts do different jobs and each one matters.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Excuse me, could you tell me the way to the station?
Excuse me, where is the post office, please?
Excuse me, is there a bank near here?

  Excuse me   opens the conversation
  could you   softer than can you
  please      goes at the end

Then — and this is the part people forget:
  So, straight on and then left at the lights?
grammar.workedExample:
You need the post office and you do not know if there is one nearby.
1. Open with excuse me. Without it, a question to a stranger sounds abrupt.
2. Choose the question. You do not know whether one exists, so ask that first: is there a post office near here?
3. If yes, then ask the way: could you tell me the way?
4. When they answer, repeat it back: so, past the bank and then right?
Result: Excuse me, is there a post office near here? … Could you tell me the way? … So, past the bank and then right?
Asking whether it exists before asking the way saves a whole exchange when the answer is no.
grammar.commonMistake: Leaving off excuse me. The question is grammatically perfect and lands badly, because English uses that phrase to open the conversation rather than to apologise. The other omission is the repeat-back, which costs three seconds and saves ten minutes of walking.
grammar.memoryTip: Excuse me opens it. Repeating it back closes it.

teacherNotes.note: The imperative comes from Units 3 and 6, static position from Unit 2, ordinals from Unit 4, and left and right are Unit 3 vocabulary recycled rather than re-listed. teacherNotes.note: Reading 2 is worth taking seriously as advice rather than as a reading text. Learners giving directions default to distances because numbers feel safer than nouns, and distances are much harder to follow. Pushing them towards go past the school rather than go for two hundred metres improves both their directions and their listening.

teacherNotes.note: Speaking 5 is built so the learner repeats a route back slightly wrong and gets corrected, because that is what the habit is for. Learners who see the correction happen once tend to adopt it; learners who are only told to do it tend not to.

teacherNotes.note: Four of the ten comprehension questions require combining a condition with a route — a month, a time, an access need. Noticing a conflict is a harder skill than following a step and worth the time.

1. along  2. past  3. across  4. through  5. towards  6. round

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
Go along this street.
Go past the bank.
Cross at the traffic lights.
Take the first turning on the left.
It is opposite the post office.
The position must be last. The order of the middle steps could vary — crossing before or after the bank both work — but going along the street has to come first and the position has to come last.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1. Excuse me, could you tell me the way to the station?
2. Excuse me, is there a bank near here?
3. Is it far from here? (or: How far is it?)
4. So, straight on, past the school, and then left at the lights?
5. Sorry — just the first part? Where do I go first?
Number 5 is the most useful sentence on this card. Asking for less is a real skill and most people give too much because they are trying to help.

1. along  2. past  3. across  4. through  5. towards  6. round  7. along  8. past  9. through  10. towards  11. round  12. across
Each word appears twice. The pairs to check are 1 and 7 against 3 and 12 — along follows the length of something, across gets you to the other side of it. And 4 and 9 are both through, because both mean in at one side and out at the other.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
MOVING: 1, 3, 5, 7. STILL: 2, 4, 6, 8.
The still ones use the Unit 2 words — next to, opposite, behind, on. The moving ones use this unit's words and the imperative.
A route uses both, and in a fixed order: the moving ones first, the still one last. That is Pattern 2.

Leave the station by the south exit.
Go along Station Road.
Go past the car park.
Cross at the traffic lights.
Take the second turning on the right.

Two things are fixed: leaving the station must be first, and the position must be last. The middle four could vary a little — crossing before or after the car park would both work — so check your answer by asking whether each step is possible at that point, not whether it matches mine exactly.

1. Excuse me, could you tell me the way to the station?
2. Excuse me, is there a post office near here?
3. Is it far from here?
4. So, straight on, past the school, and then left at the lights?

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
No key — they are your directions.
What almost everybody finds: one step assumes something only you know. A turning you take without thinking, a shortcut, a building you recognise but never named. Those are the lines to rewrite.
The second common finding is that the position at the end is not specific enough. It is on the left is not enough on a street with forty doors. Say which side, what is next to it, and what colour the door is.

Asking about somewhere you already know is deliberate — it removes the pressure entirely, so you can pay attention to the language rather than to finding the place.
What most people find: the repeat-back produced a small correction, or a piece of extra information that was not in the first answer. That extra piece is usually the most useful part, and it only appears because you repeated.
